body.text: The 'taboo' condition facing 1 in 1,000 Australian mothers
Clary Garrett now knows what was happening to her was psychosis.
As COVID-19 forced the world into lockdown, the then-21-year-old's first pregnancy sent her mental health spiralling.
She had moved back in with her mum and her son's father was no longer in the picture.
"I was at this point where I was depressed and suicidal," she says.
At 35 weeks, she suffered reduced fetal movement and bleeding, leading to her pregnancy being labelled high-risk.
"It got to the point where I was so paranoid that my baby was actually dead inside me, or dying," she says.
"I was like, 'I'm going to perform my own C-section if you don't get this baby out of me.'"
For many mums, being pregnant and giving birth can be one of the happiest times in their life.
But for one or two in every 1,000, it is the start of a mental health emergency.
Warning: This article includes content that may be distressing for some readers.
Before her son was born, Clary Garrett had never even held a baby.
After he arrived, she was going home with a newborn who had spent four weeks in special care.
"That's when things started to change," she says.
She became more paranoid. She stopped sleeping.
Her mother, she thought, was hiding her son's things — a belief that escalated until Clary believed her mother was out to steal the baby.
"I thought I was being stalked, and I thought Donald Trump was going to start a world war and bomb the tiny little town we lived in," she says.
"From there I started hearing voices.
"I started having these delusions that I had done the wrong thing by having a baby, and that my son was going to live this horrible life, because the world was so terrible.
"[I thought] the only way I could save him was by taking his life … and then killing myself."
One moment of lucidity saved her son's life, and her own.
Clary called her caseworker and told her what was going on.
She was admitted to a mother and baby unit the next day, and ultimately diagnosed with postpartum anxiety, depression and psychosis.
But she didn't find out about her psychosis diagnosis, she says, until a private psychiatrist read her medical notes.
"It was almost like it was taboo," she says.
"They didn't want to give me that label. They didn't want to put a name to it.
"I knew about baby blues, but nobody told me you can genuinely lose your mind during and after pregnancy.
"You can have your mind turn against you and not be in control of yourself."
The ABC spoke to almost a dozen women for this story. Many said they had never heard of postpartum psychosis before it became their reality.

Postpartum psychosis affects one to two in every 1,000 new mothers and is considered a psychiatric emergency, according to the Centre of Perinatal Excellence, Australia's peak body in perinatal mental health.
For those who have been diagnosed with bipolar or schizo-affective disorder, that risk factor can be as high as a 50 per cent.

[I] could no longer distinguish dream from reality ... I also experienced hallucinations. Voices in my head forced me to make choices, including a command asking whether I or my daughter should die. — Anonymous

The psychosis was completely debilitating and life-shattering, and followed by a very dark depression that nearly killed me. I still carry guilt to this day — for what my partner went through, for what my family overseas went through, for the attention I didn't give my firstborn in those precious months. — Rosie, Hobart

My son was only five weeks old and since his birth my thoughts and behaviours had very rapidly and dramatically become increasingly erratic. I didn't know it at the time but I had completely lost touch with reality. The things I believed, the hallucinations I saw and the voices I heard as part of my delusions were real to me, but to everyone else they made no sense. — Jacqueline Kirkman, Geelong

I knew something was wrong. I wasn't acting normal, but I thought I was just in acute trauma. I couldn't sleep, stayed by my little one's side at all times ... I was hypervigilant about the baby camera. I was deep cleaning instead of having a nap, I was filming my baby sleeping for two hours straight after midnight while "talking to him" about life in 2023. — Hannah, Hunter region
Leanne McGregor first started experiencing "spiritual phenomena" during childbirth with her daughter 15 years ago.
A Gold Coast-based psychologist who once worked for the Gold Coast Acute Care Team, she said she had sensed her grandparents were in the room.
She started sensing she could connect with the deceased family of her midwives.
"My partner said to one of the midwives that there was something wrong, that I was going crazy," she says.
"And the midwife said some women have really spiritual experiences during childbirth."
Her partner called a former colleague for help, but by then Leanne had given birth and left the hospital.
"I was discharged [after] five days from the maternity ward, went home and started to think that I had telepathic powers," she says.
"I put my five-day-old baby down in front of my Rottweiler. My mum was petrified and I just said, 'It's okay, I've got control of it all.'"
When she refused to go back to the hospital for help, the police were called.
"I didn't think there was a risk, because I didn't think there was anything wrong with me, other than that I needed sleep," she says.
But by midnight, she was taken via ambulance from the Gold Coast to a hospital in Ipswich.
"But my baby was removed from me [so] my mum and partner had to drive around the Gold Coast trying to find a chemist open to get formula," Leanne says.
"And then I woke up in the morning … in a glass room, and I thought I'd dreamt that I'd had a baby."
Her experience set off a struggle with mental illness that ebbed and flowed for years, continuing even when her daughter started school.
"I had a year off work where I wasn't able to get out of bed, basically," she says.

"I'd get up, drive her to school, come back home, lay in bed all day, get up, go pick her up, and then have to make small talk with all the school mums so she could have a play, then go home, get her sorted and go back to bed."
In 2018, Leanne finally found a new medication that worked.
Now, she has her own private practice and her daughter is 15 years old.
After their son was born, Gemma Tamock and her husband were elated.
They went dancing. They played music together. They invited friends over to celebrate, and cooked a banquet.
Gemma "fell in love instantly".
Then 48 years old, she had fallen pregnant via egg donation, and her son was born early due to slow growth.
"I couldn't breastfeed, but I had this crazy regimen where I had to try and express and then try to feed naturally, then feed with a bottle," she says.
"And I couldn't sleep anyway because I was scared.
"I would lie there and watch him breathe … I think fear started creeping in that something was wrong.
"But I was so excited. I thought he was so amazing, I was in love."
Two weeks in, she heard a voice she described as her own, telling her that her husband was trying to keep the baby from her.
A few days later, when she tried to feed the baby, it seemed like all the bottles in the house weren't working.
"I changed the [bottle] top for another top, that didn't seem to work, and I changed it and changed it," Gemma says.
"It was like, 'None of them work, I can't feed my child, I am a terrible mother, I'm not really his mother at all because he isn't really mine … I do not deserve this child.'
"I called the newborn care line … and the midwife, Lenore … I think she saved my life."
She describes cornering her husband afterwards, unable to stop talking, until finally he called the midwife back.
By the following day, they were in the emergency department, and that night Gemma was admitted to the acute mental health unit.
"Then I started hearing external voices that I thought were talking about me," she says.
"I didn't realise I was ill. I thought it was a misunderstanding because Joe and I had argued.
"In the hospital, I googled postnatal depression and tried to fake the symptoms."
She found couldn't read the clock on the wall and could no longer read the paperwork put in front of her.
"I said, 'I don't want to sign something that I can't understand,'" she says, her voice becoming thick with emotion.
"And [my husband] grabbed me by my hands and really looked at me and said, 'Babe, I need you to do this so that I can advocate for you.'"
Almost a decade later, Gemma can see how her thoughts "could have led somewhere really catastrophic" if not picked up on quickly.
"In the early stages, [women with postpartum psychosis] do or say something that shows a partner or family member there's something not right," she says.
"We need to take that seriously, and the thing we can't do is expect the woman to advocate for herself.
"She's hiding a fear of something you can't understand."
After a high-risk pregnancy with twin boys, Katrina Weynberg stopped sleeping.
Her sons had stopped growing at 33 weeks and were delivered prematurely, then whisked away to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).
Within hours, Katrina's heart was racing. Over the next few days, she became hyperactive, hypervigilant, and started having delusions.
"At 12 days postpartum, I was triaged into the emergency department and diagnosed with postpartum psychosis," she says.
"My husband noticed that there was something happening, and he flagged it … with the nurse unit manager of the NICU.
"Next thing I know, I'm walking down to the emergency department to be assessed."
At that point, she thought she only needed to rest, before being told she would be kept in her ward room for treatment.
"I think it wasn't until medication had finally started doing its thing that I was able to have proper conversations and have them explain to me what had happened," she says.
Katrina says she had been able to recognise the signs that something was wrong, but didn't have a name for what had happened.
"We're only talking about [postpartum psychosis] when it's a crisis," she says.
"Why is it not a mainstream topic of conversation?
"Prior to the diagnoses, I was educated, I finished a degree, and then in the end I was hospitalised after giving birth to my kids, because I had no real education about what was happening to me."
Before becoming pregnant, Amanda Potter had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.
Postpartum psychosis had been on the radar for her and her psychiatrist — like "rolling the dice".
During her first pregnancy, she had been diagnosed with postnatal depression and anxiety, and had had to stop taking her medication.
She was still in recovery when she fell pregnant with her second daughter in early 2022.
Close to her due date, Amanda suffered an acute psychotic meltdown.
"I genuinely am surprised, and my husband's genuinely surprised, that my youngest and I made it alive," she says.
"I was incredibly suicidal. I had even tried to self-induce at home at times.
"My husband and my mum had to keep reminding me that I was unwell. My psychiatrist kept a very close eye on me.
"And then when I gave birth dead-on 37 weeks, the second she came out I just took an antipsychotic.
"That's when it all hit me that I'd been so unwell for the last eight months."
Despite still facing stigma after her ordeal, Amanda decided she never wanted another mum to go through such an experience alone.

[When] our son turned five, after a lot of healing [my husband and I] felt ready and we decided to expand our family. This May we welcomed a little girl. She is an absolute delight and now we can't imagine life without her. — Jacqueline Kirkman, Geelong

I share my story to not only reduce stigma and raise awareness of what the signs are, but the importance of access to perinatal expertise and the hope the system will progress to better respond. We shouldn't have to pay thousands to see someone privately; the public system should increase resources to offer perinatal care during this acute period. — Hannah, Hunter region

We give so much of ourselves for our babies, don't we? But if you're not looking after yourself, your baby ultimately is going to suffer. So if there's anything intrusive creeping into your thought patterns and you're not behaving as your true self ... this is a mental health emergency. — Beck, Perth

For women and families going through it right now, I want my story to offer genuine hope. Recovery is entirely possible, and you can come out the other side equipped with new strength, resilience and positive tools for life. — Anonymous

When such an illness is attached to motherhood, the incomprehension and incredulity is multiplied. [Because] as a society, we believe women are inherently programmed to love, nurture and protect above all else … And when things don’t turn out that way, it is seen as 'abnormal', as 'unnatural'. — Rosie, Hobart
Last year Amanda founded The Held Project, an organisation delivering peer support to mothers in Mackay flagged as a potential perinatal or postnatal mental health risk.
The team includes a social worker, an endorsed midwife, registered nurse and a postpartum doula.

"I remember thinking, 'I just want another mum who's been through this to bring me a coffee and sit and tell me I'm not a bad mum … that I don't want to hurt myself and I don't want to hurt my baby,'" she says.
Once a mum has requested a visit, the project's ambassadors arrive with wellbeing bags of essentials, care items, a coffee and a listening ear.
Amanda's daughters, Sarah and Georgie, now aged six and four, help her pack each bag.
"I'm going to visit a mum today," she says.
"She's got a little boy, she's three months postpartum and she's not doing good.
"The girls are so aware of it, they help me pack these bags and say, 'Oh, I hope this makes the mum feel so much better, Mummy.'"
